How effectively can LSTM networks predict impending software-system failures from multivariate telemetry

This is the capstone project of IDC6910 class

Author

Duc Nguyen, Luis Madrigal (Advisor: Dr. Cohen)

Published

November 3, 2026

Slides: slides.html ( Go to slides.qmd to edit)

Introduction

Modern software systems generate large amounts of telemetry data, including performance metrics, logs, and other operational signals. This information may contain early warning signs of system failures; however, detecting those signs can be challenging, especially in complex systems. Improving failure prediction can help organizations respond earlier, reduce system downtime and associated costs, and improve overall system reliability.

This project will use Microsoft’s OpenRCA dataset (Xu et al. 2025a) to investigate whether Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) neural networks can predict impending software-system failures from system telemetry. Because LSTMs are designed to learn patterns over time, they may be useful for detecting changes in telemetry data that occur before a system failure. We will evaluate how accurately failures can be predicted at different time horizons and whether combining multiple telemetry sources improves prediction performance compared with using a single source. Overall, this project applies machine learning to a practical software reliability problem by testing the effectiveness of telemetry data for early failure detection.

Previous research is supportive of using LSTM models in the analysis of sequential data. (Gonzalez and Yu 2018) showed that LSTM networks can be used in modeling nonlinear systems, while (Ergen and Kozat 2020) used LSTM-based methods for anomaly detection in data sequences with variable length. Other studies applied LSTMs to telemetry data obtained from computer systems. (Mudgal and Wouhaybi 2024) used a combined LSTM encoder in anomaly detection methods. These include Isolation Forest, used to identify PC system failures from CPU, memory, disk, temperature, and system data. This study obtained results that suggested LSTM-based telemetry analysis can provide useful results for system-failure detection.

System log research also shows how important sequential modeling can be in failure-related tasks. (Chen, Luktarhan, and Lv 2022) used two LSTM networks in the analysis of events before and after a log entry; this improved anomaly detection in long log sequences. In addition, (Hadadi et al. 2024) researched deep learning for log-based failure prediction and found that model performance is dependent on how log data are represented and transformed into sequences. The OpenRCA dataset will be particularly useful in this project as it contains real failure case data from enterprise systems, with multiple sources of telemetry, such as logs, metrics, and traces (Xu et al. 2025b). While the prior work mentioned mainly focused on anomaly detection or cause analysis, this project will be more focused on predicting failures before they occur and testing the efficacy of multiple telemetry sources in improving early failure prediction performance.

Methods

A Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network is a type of recurrent neural network (RNN) designed to learn from sequential data while retaining useful information over time. As it processes each time step, the LSTM updates a cell state that carries information forward. Three gates control this process: the forget gate determines what information to retain, the input gate determines what new information to add, and the output gate determines what information to expose to the next time step. This gating structure helps the network learn which patterns of change over time are useful for making predictions (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997).

We chose an LSTM because it can learn from the order of telemetry measurements over time. Some faults may be preceded by gradual changes in metrics, such as increasing memory use or CPU utilization that remains elevated. By processing a recent sequence of measurements, the model can learn whether these patterns help predict a fault before it begins. This section explains how the LSTM processes sequences, the assumptions behind our modeling approach, how we prepare OpenRCA telemetry for the model, and how we train it.

Recurrent Neural Networks and the Vanishing Gradient

A recurrent neural network processes a sequence \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_T\) one step at a time. At each step it combines the current input \(x_t\) with a hidden state \(h_{t-1}\) that summarizes everything it has seen so far:

\[ h_t = \tanh\left(W x_t + U h_{t-1} + b\right) \tag{1}\]

The same weights \(W\), \(U\) and \(b\) are reused at every time step, so the network can handle a sequence of any length with a fixed number of parameters.

RNNs are trained with backpropagation through time (BPTT) (Werbos 1990): the network is “unrolled” over the sequence, and the error at the final step is passed backwards through every earlier step. The gradient that reaches step \(t-k\) contains a product of \(k\) Jacobian matrices,

\[ \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-k}} = \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t} \operatorname{diag}\!\left(1 - h_j^2\right) U . \tag{2}\]

When the terms in this product are smaller than one, the gradient shrinks exponentially as \(k\) grows (it vanishes); when they are larger than one, it grows exponentially (it explodes) (Bengio, Simard, and Frasconi 1994; Pascanu, Mikolov, and Bengio 2013). In practice, a plain RNN therefore learns only short-range patterns. For our problem, this is a serious limitation: an early warning sign 20 minutes before a fault is 20 steps back in the sequence.

Mathematical Foundations of the LSTM

The LSTM replaces the single update in Equation 1 with a memory cell \(c_t\) and three gates. Following the standard formulation with a forget gate (Gers, Schmidhuber, and Cummins 2000), the computation at each time step \(t\) is:

\[ \begin{aligned} f_t &= \sigma\left(W_f x_t + U_f h_{t-1} + b_f\right) && \text{forget gate}\\ i_t &= \sigma\left(W_i x_t + U_i h_{t-1} + b_i\right) && \text{input gate}\\ o_t &= \sigma\left(W_o x_t + U_o h_{t-1} + b_o\right) && \text{output gate}\\ \tilde{c}_t &= \tanh\left(W_c x_t + U_c h_{t-1} + b_c\right) && \text{candidate memory}\\ c_t &= f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t && \text{cell state update}\\ h_t &= o_t \odot \tanh\left(c_t\right) && \text{hidden state (output)} \end{aligned} \tag{3}\]

where:

  • \(x_t\) is the input vector at time \(t\): the telemetry readings for one minute.
  • \(h_{t-1}\) is the hidden state from the previous minute; \(h_t\) is the new one.
  • \(c_{t-1}\) and \(c_t\) are the old and new cell states — the long-term memory.
  • \(f_t\), \(i_t\), \(o_t\) are the gates. Each is a vector of numbers between 0 and 1 produced by the logistic sigmoid \(\sigma(z) = 1/(1+e^{-z})\). A value near 0 means “block” and a value near 1 means “let through”.
  • \(\tilde{c}_t\) is the candidate memory: new information that could be written to the cell. The \(\tanh\) function keeps it between \(-1\) and \(1\).
  • \(W_\ast\) are the input weight matrices, \(U_\ast\) are the recurrent weight matrices, and \(b_\ast\) are bias vectors, one set for each gate and the candidate.
  • \(\odot\) is element-wise (Hadamard) multiplication.

What each gate does.

  • The forget gate \(f_t\) decides how much of the old memory \(c_{t-1}\) to keep. If a component of \(f_t\) is close to 1, that part of the memory is carried forward; close to 0, it is erased.
  • The input gate \(i_t\) decides how much of the candidate \(\tilde{c}_t\) is written into memory. This lets the network ignore minutes that carry no useful information.
  • The output gate \(o_t\) decides how much of the memory is exposed in the hidden state \(h_t\), which is what the next step — and eventually the prediction layer — sees.

Why this fixes the vanishing gradient. The key line in Equation 3 is the cell update \(c_t = f_t \odot c_{t-1} + i_t \odot \tilde{c}_t\). It is additive, not a repeated squashing like Equation 1. Along this path, the gradient from one step to the previous is

\[ \frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t), \]

so as long as the network learns to keep the forget gate open (\(f_t \approx 1\)), the error signal can travel back across many time steps without shrinking. This is the “constant error carousel” that gives the LSTM its long memory (Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997).

Matrix and Vector Dimensions

Let \(k\) be the number of input features and \(d\) the number of hidden units. Then:

Symbol Dimension Meaning
\(x_t\) \(k \times 1\) telemetry at minute \(t\)
\(h_t,\; c_t,\; f_t,\; i_t,\; o_t,\; \tilde{c}_t\) \(d \times 1\) hidden state, cell state, gates, candidate
\(W_f, W_i, W_o, W_c\) \(d \times k\) input weights
\(U_f, U_i, U_o, U_c\) \(d \times d\) recurrent weights
\(b_f, b_i, b_o, b_c\) \(d \times 1\) biases

The four weight sets are usually stacked into one matrix, so a single LSTM layer has

\[ 4\left(dk + d^2 + d\right) \]

trainable parameters. In this project, the input has \(k = 128\) selected telemetry features and the LSTM has \(d = 64\) hidden units, which gives \(4(64 \cdot 128 + 64^2 + 64) = 49{,}408\) parameters in the LSTM layer. (PyTorch keeps two bias vectors per gate, which adds another \(4d = 256\).) The prediction layer described below adds \(d + 1 = 65\) more, for a total of \(49{,}729\) parameters. Importantly, this number does not depend on the length of the sequence: the same weights are applied at every minute.

Example

To make Equation 3 concrete, consider a toy LSTM with \(d = 1\) hidden unit that watches \(k = 2\) scaled telemetry features of one container: CPU usage and memory usage. At the previous minute, the network’s state was \(h_{t-1} = 0.2\) and \(c_{t-1} = 0.5\). At the current minute, CPU usage spikes while memory is normal:

\[ x_t = \begin{bmatrix} \text{CPU} \\ \text{Memory} \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1.5 \\ 0.3 \end{bmatrix} \]

Suppose training has produced the following weights:

Gate \(W_\ast\) (CPU, Memory) \(U_\ast\) \(b_\ast\)
forget \(f\) \([\,0.6,\; -0.2\,]\) 0.5 1.0
input \(i\) \([\,0.8,\; 0.1\,]\) 0.3 0.0
output \(o\) \([\,0.4,\; 0.2\,]\) 0.6 0.2
candidate \(\tilde{c}\) \([\,0.9,\; 0.3\,]\) 0.4 \(-0.1\)

Step 1 — gates. For the forget gate,

\[ f_t = \sigma(0.6 \cdot 1.5 - 0.2 \cdot 0.3 + 0.5 \cdot 0.2 + 1.0) = \sigma(1.94) = 0.874 . \]

The other gates follow in the same way:

\[ i_t = \sigma(1.29) = 0.784, \qquad o_t = \sigma(0.98) = 0.727, \qquad \tilde{c}_t = \tanh(1.42) = 0.890 . \]

Step 2 — update the memory.

\[ c_t = \underbrace{0.874 \times 0.5}_{\text{kept from before}} + \underbrace{0.784 \times 0.890}_{\text{newly written}} = 0.437 + 0.698 = 1.135 \]

Step 3 — produce the output.

\[ h_t = 0.727 \times \tanh(1.135) = 0.727 \times 0.813 = 0.591 \]

The network kept most of its earlier memory (87 %) and added a large new contribution because the CPU spike opened the input gate. The value of \(c_t\) has grown from 0.5 to 1.135, so the “something unusual is happening” signal will be carried into the next minutes. Repeating these three steps for every minute of the look-back window is all the LSTM does; training consists of finding weights that make this memory useful for predicting failures.

From a Sequence to a Failure Prediction

For each minute \(t\) we give the LSTM the previous \(L = 60\) minutes of telemetry, \(x_{t-59}, \dots, x_t\), and run Equation 3 over them in order. Only the final hidden state \(h_t\) is used for the prediction, because by then it summarizes the whole window. It passes through dropout and a single linear layer, and a sigmoid turns the result into a probability:

\[ \hat{p}_t = \sigma\!\left(v^{\top} \operatorname{Dropout}(h_t) + b_v\right), \tag{4}\]

where \(v\) is a \(d \times 1\) weight vector and \(b_v\) is a scalar. \(\hat{p}_t\) is the model’s estimated probability that a failure will start within the next \(H\) minutes.

Parameter Estimation

The parameters \(\theta = \{W_\ast, U_\ast, b_\ast, v, b_v\}\) are learned by minimizing a weighted binary cross-entropy loss over the \(N\) training windows:

\[ \mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^{N} \Big[\, w_{+}\, y_n \log \hat{p}_n + (1 - y_n)\log\left(1 - \hat{p}_n\right) \Big] \tag{5}\]

where \(y_n \in \{0, 1\}\) is the true label. Failures are rare, so the positive-class weight \(w_{+}\) is set to the ratio of negative to positive windows in the training data. Without this weight the model could reach a low loss by always predicting “no failure”.

Gradients of Equation 5 are computed by backpropagation through time and the weights are updated with the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba 2015), which adapts the step size for each parameter. Several standard techniques keep training stable and reduce overfitting:

  • Gradient clipping. If the overall gradient norm exceeds 5 it is rescaled to 5. This guards against the exploding-gradient problem described above (Pascanu, Mikolov, and Bengio 2013).
  • Dropout with rate 0.2 on the final hidden state randomly zeroes units during training, so the prediction cannot rely on any single unit (Srivastava et al. 2014).
  • Weight decay of \(10^{-5}\) adds a small L2 penalty on the weights.
  • Early stopping. After each epoch the model is scored on a separate validation set. Training stops when the validation score has not improved for 4 epochs, and the weights from the best epoch are restored.

Analysis and Results

Dataset Description

The data come from OpenRCA (Xu et al. 2025a), a public benchmark released by Microsoft for root-cause analysis of software failures. OpenRCA collects telemetry from three enterprise microservice systems: Bank, Telecom and Market (the last split into two deployments, cloudbed-1 and cloudbed-2), into which engineers deliberately injected faults such as CPU exhaustion, memory leaks and network delays. For every system, OpenRCA provides:

  • Telemetry, organised into one folder per day, with three modalities:
    • metrics — numeric key performance indicators (KPIs) such as CPU use, memory use, response time, and request counts, sampled every few seconds to minutes;
    • logs — text messages written by the services;
    • traces — records of individual requests travelling between services.
  • A fault record (record.csv) listing every injected fault with its start time, the component it was injected into, and the type of fault.

Scope of this study. We focus on the Bank and Telecom systems and on their metric telemetry only. We chose these two systems because:

  1. Each is a single, self-contained system with one fault record, so the telemetry and the labels line up directly. Market is split into two separate deployments that would each need their own pipeline.
  2. They are very different from each other — different business domains, numbers of components, monitoring tools and time periods — so a result that holds on both is more convincing than a result on one.
  3. Metrics are numeric time series that can be placed on a common one-minute grid, which is the input the LSTM needs. Logs and traces would first require text parsing and request-level aggregation, which is outside the scope of this project.

All OpenRCA timestamps are Unix epoch values, and all dates and day-folder names are in UTC+8 (China Standard Time). Dates and times in this report are shown in UTC+8.

Variable Description

The fault record has the same columns in both systems:

The record gives each fault’s start time only; it does not say how long the fault lasted. This is important for labeling, described below.

The metric files come in two layouts:

Each combination of a component and a KPI — for example Tomcat04 ‖ CPU utilisation — is one time series, and becomes one input feature for the model.

library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)

The fault records are small and are loaded directly. Start times are converted from epoch seconds to UTC+8 date-times.

              component,
              reason,
              timestamp = as.numeric(timestamp),
              onset     = as.POSIXct(timestamp, origin = "1970-01-01",
                                     tz = "Asia/Shanghai"))   # UTC+8
}

Bank has faults on 9 of its 10 days and Telecom on 11 of its 15 days. The days with telemetry but no recorded faults (Bank 2021-03-05; Telecom 2020-04-20 to 2020-04-23) are kept in the data as fault-free periods.

The metric telemetry is much larger — about 16 GB for Telecom and roughly 90 MB per day for Bank — so it is not stored in this repository. It is read day by day in Python with pandas. The function below reads one metric file and turns it into a table with one row per minute and one column per component‖KPI series; the long and wide layouts in Table 4 are handled separately:

def load_source(day_dir, src, grid):
    """Read one metric file into a minute x feature table ('component||kpi')."""
    if src.kind == "long":
        df = pd.read_csv(day_dir / src.path,
                         usecols=[src.ts_col, src.id_col, src.kpi_col, src.val_col])
        df["minute"] = to_minute(df[src.ts_col], src.ts_unit)   # s or ms -> minute
        df["feature"] = df[src.id_col] + "||" + df[src.kpi_col]
        wide = df.pivot_table(index="minute", columns="feature",
                              values=src.val_col, aggfunc="mean")
    else:  # wide layout (metric_app.csv)
        df = pd.read_csv(day_dir / src.path)
        df["minute"] = to_minute(df[src.ts_col], src.ts_unit)
        wide = pd.concat([df.pivot_table(index="minute", columns=src.id_col,
                                         values=v, aggfunc="mean")
                            .add_prefix("app||").add_suffix("." + v)
                          for v in src.value_cols], axis=1)
    return wide.reindex(grid)          # exact 1-minute grid for that day

Running this for every metric file and every day produces the raw feature tables:

The high share of missing cells is expected: many KPIs are recorded every 2 minutes or once an hour rather than every minute, so most of their cells on a 1-minute grid are empty.

Data Preparation and Labeling

Cleaning the telemetry

The raw tables are cleaned in four steps:

  1. Align to a 1-minute grid. Every reading is assigned to the minute it falls in, and readings within the same minute are averaged. Each day becomes exactly 1,440 (Bank) or 360 (Telecom) rows. Telecom timestamps are first divided by 1,000 to convert milliseconds to seconds.
  2. Keep only series present on every day. A model cannot use a feature that disappears halfway through the data. Some Bank containers (dockerA1, dockerA2, dockerB1, dockerB2) stop reporting by 2021-03-24, which removes 248 series; Telecom loses 430 series this way.
  3. Drop sparse series. Any series more than 80 % missing on the 1-minute grid is removed; there is too little data to fill it reliably.
  4. Fill short gaps. Within each day, a missing value is filled with the last observed value (or, at the start of a day, the next one), but only for up to twice that series’ own sampling interval, and at least 2 minutes. A KPI sampled every 2 minutes can therefore be filled for up to 4 minutes, while a longer outage in the data is not hidden. Gaps are never filled across days.

The few missing values that remain after filling are set to 0 before the data are scaled and windowed (see the Methods section).

Labeling

The fault record gives a start time for each fault, but our goal is to predict a fault before it starts. We therefore turn each fault into labels on the minutes leading up to it. For a prediction horizon of \(H\) minutes, the label of minute \(t\) is

\[ y_{t,H} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if any fault starts in the interval } (t,\; t + H],\\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \tag{6}\]

In words, minute \(t\) is positive if a failure will begin within the next \(H\) minutes. We build labels for six horizons, \(H \in \{1, 3, 5, 10, 15, 30\}\) minutes, so we can measure how prediction quality changes as the model is asked to look further ahead. Fault start times are rounded down to the minute so that they fall on the same grid as the telemetry. All 136 Bank and 51 Telecom faults land on the grid.

Two further rules decide which minutes can be used at all:

  • Blackout after a fault. The record does not say how long a fault lasts. For the 10 minutes after a fault starts, the system is probably still failing, so these minutes are removed from the negative examples. Otherwise the model would be rewarded for “predicting” a fault that is already visible in the telemetry.
  • Complete windows only. A minute is used only if its full 60-minute look-back window and its \(H\)-minute look-ahead both lie on the same day. The recorded days are not consecutive — for example, Bank jumps from 2021-03-12 to 2021-03-23 — so a window that crossed midnight would join two unrelated days together.

These rules remove the first hour of every day and a few minutes around each fault. Table 7 shows the result: the number of usable minutes and the share labelled positive at each horizon.

Three points stand out:

  • Positives are rare at short horizons. At \(H = 1\) only about 1 % of minutes are positive. A model that always predicts “no failure” would be 99 % accurate, which is why we evaluate with PR-AUC rather than accuracy.
  • The two systems are directly comparable. Both have about 9.4 faults per 1,000 minutes, so their positive rates are almost identical at every horizon.
  • The real sample size is the number of faults. Positive minutes next to each other belong to the same fault and are not independent. Bank has 136 fault events and Telecom only 51, so Telecom results will be less certain.

Figure 2 summarises each system: faults per day, faults by injected reason, the share of missing minutes per series before and after gap-filling, and the positive rate at each prediction horizon.
